title: Al-Humazah: the slanderer
hook: woe to the backbiter who counts his money and thinks it will keep him (Surah 104)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Al-Fil, the army of the elephant, and a grandfather who asked for his camels. Your line was the house was defended. Day one hundred seventy.

He turns up at work, at school, at family dinners. The one doing impressions of a coworker the moment she leaves the room. The eye-roll across the table. The group-chat screenshot with a laughing emoji. It feels small, and it feels safe, especially when you have more money, more status, more followers. Today's surah has a word for this person, and it doesn't treat it as small at all. Nine lines, and it opens with woe.
screen: `THE IMPRESSION BEHIND HER BACK.` → `THE EYE-ROLL, THE SCREENSHOT.` → `IT OPENS WITH WOE.`

segments.voice: Surah one hundred four begins, in Pickthall's translation: Woe unto every slandering traducer, Who hath gathered wealth of this world and arrangeth it. He thinketh that his wealth will render him immortal. In Arabic the first line is two sharp words: humazah, lumazah. Commentators give them related shades. One mocks with gestures: the look, the smirk, the pointed finger. The other wounds with the tongue, especially behind someone's back. Both make someone smaller so you can feel bigger. Then the surah moves straight from mockery to money. The mocker is also the man counting his wealth, over and over, arranging it. In the surah's picture, contempt for people and trust in money come from the same place: the belief that you're safe, above it all, untouchable. He thinks his wealth will make him last forever. The surah says no, and describes a fire that reaches the heart, where the contempt began. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ gave a plain definition of backbiting, recorded in Sahih Muslim. He asked his companions: do you know what backbiting is? It's mentioning your brother in a way he would dislike. Someone asked: what if it's true? He said: if it's true, that's backbiting. If it's false, that's slander. So the test isn't whether the joke is accurate. It's whether they'd be hurt to hear it. Money won't keep you. Neither will the laugh at someone else's expense.
screen: `HUMAZAH, LUMAZAH — THE LOOK, THE TONGUE.` · `FROM MOCKERY STRAIGHT TO MONEY.` · `HE THINKS HIS WEALTH WILL KEEP HIM.` · `EVEN IF IT'S TRUE, IT'S BACKBITING.` · then, large: `MONEY WON'T KEEP YOU.`

segments.voice: Think honestly about the last time you mocked someone, out loud, in a message, or just with a look. No guilt; just see it clearly, and ask what you were protecting. Then picture that person hearing it, and let the picture be real for a moment.
Al-Humazah. The slanderer, the one who mocks and belittles; the name of Surah one hundred four. Today's word.
Your line: money won't keep you. A joke that's true can still be backbiting. One hundred seventy days now.

howItsDone: Muslims recite al-Humazah in the prayers, and Islamic teaching treats backbiting (ghibah) and slander as serious wrongs; many try to leave a gathering or change the subject when others are mocked.

trapdoor: what you thought: a surah about gossip.
what it means: mockery and trust in money grow from the same false sense of being untouchable.
what a scholar hears: humazah and lumazah are intensive forms (habitual mockers); Muslim 2589 defines ghibah; the fire 'reaching the hearts' (104:7) answers where contempt starts.
